articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI does something impossible — it lives up to the hype
articles.summary: Grand Theft Auto 5 turned into one of the biggest games ever released, and its long-awaited sequel — GTA 6 — improves on it in almost every way.
articles.body: How do you follow a game like Grand Theft Auto V? Thirteen years ago, Rockstar’s crime-fueled epic went on to redefine what an open-world game could be and became an enormous success, selling more than 230 million copies across three generations of game consoles. It sits just behind Tetris and Minecraft on the list of the best-selling games of all time, and its lucrative online mode has helped it remain popular for well over a decade. That level of success has allowed Rockstar to take its time with a sequel, which has further increased the hype around the next GTA. A series of major leaks and delays only exacerbated this. At a time when much of the video game industry is struggling, the next edition of GTA stands alone, a cultural moment so big (almost) everybody has been forced to get out of the way. The buildup to Grand Theft Auto VI’s launch is unlike anything the game industry has ever seen. Even more remarkable? The game was actually worth the wait. At this point I’ve spent nearly 80 hours in Leonida, GTA VI’s fictional take on Florida. And what I’ve experienced is a game that combines the wide-open freedom offered in GTA V with the remarkable level of immersion from the studio’s 2018 release Red Dead Redemption 2, while also improving on both qualities. At the same time, it’s also the most mature GTA game Rockstar has ever made, merging the criminal antics and absurdist humor the series is known for with a love story that gives you new ways to interact with the world and new reasons for wanting to push forward. This is the GTA game the studio has been building toward for its entire existence. [Image: Let’s start with that new premise. GTA V introduced the idea of multiple protagonists to the series, and VI takes that concept in a different direction. It’s a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired story about Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, two small-time criminals who meet while, of course, stealing a car. It’s the most GTA-possible meet-cute. The idea is that you can play as both characters individually and also build their relationship over the course of the game. Things start out relatively slow. At the outset, Lucia is in prison, and you play solely as Jason, getting things ready for when she gets out. You can fix up your ramshackle house — that involves actually nailing down new stairs and rolling out paint on the walls — and also start building up a nest egg through means that are not exactly legal. Jason and Lucia’s relationship grows naturally over the course of the game, but it’s also a slow buildup to becoming the inseparable pair they were by the end of my playthrough. GTA VI approaches most of the experience with confident and deliberate pacing. Even when you control them individually, the characters are often together, either just hanging out or partnering for a crime. And being able to play as both is one of the game’s standout features. But I didn’t get to that point in the game until almost 17 hours in. Before that, you play as both leads mostly solo, learning who they are as people, before you’re given free rein to switch between the two. --- ‘It’s a risk’: How Rockstar built the most detailed (and romantic) GTA yet [Image: --- What’s great about the premise is how seamlessly it fits with what you’re actually doing in the game. There’s some bigger-picture stuff that I won’t spoil, but generally speaking, the main goal in GTA VI is to make a lot of money so that Jason and Lucia can get out of the criminal life for good and retire somewhere comfortably. And outside of the big story missions, you’re largely free to choose how you go about that. You can rob jewelry stores, steal cars, raid drug dens, or even search for hidden treasure at the bottom of the sea. Over the course of the game you’ll also meet different criminals who serve as fences, so you can sell them whatever you’ve got to build up your savings account. Sometimes they’ll even text you targets that are particularly lucrative. The structure feels natural and gives you a lot of freedom in how you play. I’m not a big fan of armed robbery, for instance. There are just so many things that can go wrong, and I almost always end up killing some innocent bystander when I try to escape. But I love getaway chases, and so stealing cars became my main form of income. Most importantly, though, this structure gives you a lot of reasons to go out in the world and explore. The missions take you all over the map — which is actually entirely accessible from the very beginning, if you choose to play that way — including not only the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City, but also tourist beaches, swamps, trailer parks, and a wild variety of other locations, each with its own landscape to explore and characters to meet. To be clear: Despite being larger, more mature, and more lifelike, this is still very much GTA. This is a game about chaos and crime. This comes across in a few ways. First, there are those smaller missions where you never really know how things will play out. The cashier at the pawn shop you’re robbing might have a shotgun, or you might accidentally smash into a big rig during a high-speed getaway. The world itself is full of unpredictable moments that force you to think on your feet. Several times I stopped my car to talk to an NPC whose vehicle broke down on the side of the road. In one instance the driver just swore at me to leave her alone. In another, I got pulled into an entire storyline involving a delivery driver who needed help to keep her AI chatbot manager off her back. I delivered her packages and ended up dealing with everything from porch pirates to tigers. There are also the multistep heists, which return from GTA V more intricate and complex. These are the big scores and involve several different missions: You spend time getting the right gear and gathering all of the information you need to actually pull them off. Even some of the sub-missions can be gigantic, including one where you have to go undercover for weeks of in-game time to get everything you need in order. But the payoff is incredible. The heists play out like over-the-top action set-pieces, as if they were pulled out of a Christopher Nolan movie like Tenet or Inception (but without all of the sci-fi twists). Even better, all of the missions in the game feel streamlined with a new checkpoint system that allows you to spend less time replaying sequences after failing, and if you fail too many times, you can just skip that mission altogether. There are still a few too many prolonged shootouts, but the checkpoints mean they’re much less tedious than in past GTA games. [Image: All of this action is crammed into a world that isn’t just huge, but also feels more alive than ever before. Like in Red Dead Redemption 2, you can talk with any NPC, but here you have more options, letting you either greet them or, if you feel like causing trouble, taunt them. Most of the time you’ll get a simple “hey” or someone begging for a few dollars. Other times you’ll get pulled into a fistfight or an unexpected storyline. Once, on my way to buy new clothes, I accidentally bumped into some gang members who followed me inside the store, and I had no choice but to fight them. The owner of the shop called the cops, and so I figured if I was in this much trouble, I might as well empty the register. What started out as a quest to find a cool T-shirt turned into a high-speed escape from the cops. Another important thing to note: While the game retains the series’ satirical tone in many ways, the humor doesn’t punch down like in past GTAs, at least from what I’ve played. Instead it makes fun of stuff that deserves to be made fun of: men’s rights activists, NFT bros, conspiracy theorists, Bryan Johnson. But what really makes the world so special are all the small, meaningful details. Changing your clothes is a lot of fun, but it also helps keep the cops off your back when you’re wanted. Eating and drinking helps improve your physical abilities. And, this being GTA, you can use just about every kind of vehicle imaginable. That includes taking the bus, which runs on a predetermined route, making stops along the way. You can rent electric scooters, and just like in real life, they’re a menace clogging up the streets of Vice City. Your cars even need to be gassed up from time to time. It’s a careful balancing act. These details make the world feel more nuanced and textured, but they’re also minor enough that they don’t feel tedious. This isn’t The Sims where you’re constantly monitoring your characters’ bodily functions. Usually, I only remembered to eat when the fitness app on my phone told me I needed more protein, and I didn’t once have a car break down because I forgot to fill up the tank. These smaller mechanisms are just enough to add a sense of realism without getting in the way of the action. You can also ignore a lot of them; at no point do you need to shower, but you might hear some snide remarks from your partner if you don’t. Perhaps the best example of this is the in-game smartphone, which is integrated into the lives of both characters in a thoughtful, plausible way. Crime bosses might text you a location to meet up, for instance, and you can add it to your GPS and head over. Or Lucia might text Jason a link to a funny video, which you can then open in a social networking app, and you can even read the comments. Smartphones have become a common user interface in games, but in GTA VI it’s a part of the world; the game doesn’t pause when you pull out your phone, meaning that if you get a text while you’re driving, you can either pull over and read it or try to text and drive. I also found these details, like the phone calls and texts between the couple, pulled me further into the story of Jason and Lucia and made me feel closer to both of them. When the two are together, you can press one of the shoulder buttons to make them hold hands. As long as you keep pressing it, they stay together. At first I used this strategically, imagining that if a couple holding hands was casing a jewelry store, it would be much less conspicuous. But eventually, as I grew to know the couple, it just became a thing I did without thinking about it. These two are crazy in love; of course they’re going to hold hands all the time. You can even do little things like make a coffee and choose to hand it to your partner instead of drinking it yourself, and all of these acts improve your relationship, which in turn impacts how the characters relate to each other and how some of the narrative elements play out. You don’t have to do any of that. There are just so many ways to interact with the world that different players will find their own things to fixate on. For me, it was a lot of holding hands and drinking coffee every morning. Someone else might get really into fashion or hunting or customizing cars. I barely touched on any of those elements and still felt like I had a substantial experience. Jason and Lucia are two very different people, each with their own kinds of stories to explore within the game. The big missions are cinematic heists that usually involve some combination of the two. But there are large, branching narratives that are only playable as one or the other character. Jason, for instance, has an old friend who is trying to start a record label in the back room of a strip club. As with the best GTA stories, the tale steadily escalates until you’re feuding with a famous rapper and facing down a number of life-or-death situations. Lucia, meanwhile, has to deal with her mom’s quest to become a real estate agent that gets her caught up with a violent gang, and her best friend pulling her into a pyramid scheme that seems very much like a cult but turns out to be something even more ridiculous. These storylines are so big and absorbing that I would often forget about the main campaign for long periods of time. [Image: It’s not that there are zero issues with the game. The combat is still clunky, and the weapon wheel is still frustrating; there were multiple times when I accidentally equipped a flashlight instead of a shotgun when in the heat of battle. I also ran into a handful of small bugs, like dead bodies comically flopping around or a coffee mug that was stuck floating in a hotel room. But given how ambitious GTA VI is, and how badly things can go with large open games, the relative lack of technical issues during my playthrough is impressive. Even better: I played the game on a launch-version PS5, and it ran just fine. Back in 2018, I called Red Dead Redemption 2 “the most convincing open-world game ever made,” and over the last eight years that has remained true. There have been great examples of the form since then — Elden Ring, Tears of the Kingdom, Control Resonant, Cyberpunk 2077 (eventually) — but none that approach the scale and detail of Rockstar’s works. Certainly none that attempted to do it in anything like the contemporary, real-world setting that has made GTA so pervasive. Now that mantle has been passed to GTA VI. To give you a sense of how big this game is, despite spending more than 70 hours in the world and completing the main story, I’ve only managed to get through less than 60 percent of the total experience. And I just spent 2,500 words explaining how good GTA VI is without even touching on some of the best parts: the incredible selection of music, the hilarious talk radio stations, the pitch-perfect casting, the lifelike graphics. There are full-on TV shows, books, and video games that you can experience inside of the game. The most pretentious indie game of 2026? It exists in GTA VI. For the last decade the idea of GTA VI has been inseparable from the hype around it. All of the noise caused by leaks, delays, and the protracted development time has turned the game into something larger than life, an experience hailed as the biggest game of all time before it even launched. It really seemed like no project could live up to the level of scrutiny that GTA VI has been and will be subjected to. But now we can forget all of that, because GTA VI is actually here. And the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it. Grand Theft Auto VI launches on the PS5 and Xbox on November 19th.

articles.title: GTA 6 Review: One of the Most Impressive Video Games Ever Made, Nonstop Astonishing Across Its Unbelievably Detailed World
articles.summary: Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered.
articles.body:
During my first dozen-or-so hours with Grand Theft Auto 6, I fixed my leaky roof, collected some rum from a shady liquor store, played way too many games of pool, read a book about World War 2 soldiers with a penchant for teabagging, and caught a lot of fish. On the more ridiculous end of the spectrum, I also temporarily… borrowed a luxury yacht called Party on the Poop Deck before running it aground and drinking its owner’s beer, slapped the crap out of a bloke who cursed at me, found a finger in my horniest neighbour’s plumbing, threatened an alligator wearing a hat, and got mugged by a drunk sea captain with a harpoon gun – before stealing his weapon while he peed in a garden.

Over 100 hours later, I’ve now completely lost track of all the things I’ve seen and done within GTA 6’s astounding open world – and I see no real limit to the amount of time I could spend here, endlessly exploring and interacting with Vice City and the massive area surrounding it. While the well-paced story effectively nudged me around the map, there are still vast sections of it that I’m yet to even visit – despite hitting the credits after almost 120 hours of hijinks. Frankly, I’ve never played anything that’s hit quite like GTA 6 – and right now I have zero plans to stop playing it.

Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series. Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous GTA games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it is invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.

My Jason and Lucia maintained a professional criminal rating throughout thanks to my style of play, where I opt for clean escapes, stealth, and non-lethal takedowns against general law enforcement if feasible, disabling vehicles by popping tyres rather than pummelling the windscreens with gunfire, and leaving civilians unharmed as often as possible. By the end of the story, I had actually only killed 11 civilians, all of which would’ve been unfortunate accidents.

Jason, a capable yet calm and softly spoken army veteran, is a natural fit for GTA. He remains mostly a mystery throughout, but his quiet cowboy demeanour doesn’t stray too far from Red Dead Redemption 2 ’s Arthur Morgan, and I like that. Lucia, who’s headstrong but not abrasive and confident but not cocky, gets to showcase a wider range of emotions. She’s easily the most likeable and multifaceted woman in the history of the series, and it’s abundantly clear that GTA’s writing has grown up dramatically in the last 13 years – and that RDR2 has had nothing but positive effects on its sister series.

We play mostly as Jason for the opening phase of Chapter 1, but it’s a smart way of easing us into the many systems we need to come to grips with (there’s a full help menu to explain any controls or actions you might forget). In the time it takes to start and finish many typical shooters and action games, I’d lived several days of a second life as Jason, who spends a good deal of his time on the wrong side of the law couriering drug shipments up and down the Leonida Keys but otherwise keeps a low profile in the relatively quiet tourist town he calls home. There’d been strife and there’d been shootouts, sure, but the main thread of the story had barely begun: Lucia was yet to re-enter the picture, I’d not even visited Vice City itself at all, and I was entirely content to while away hours messing around with GTA 6’s many, many distractions.

It’s ironic, perhaps, that some of its greatest distractions are actually games themselves – Jason has a PlayStation-style console in his home featuring three playable games, and his local bar has a darkly humorous riff on classic Buck Hunter cabinets I kept getting sucked into. Straight away, it’s evident this is not a world of painted-on backdrops and empty props. This is a world that feels more lived-in and real than anything I’ve ever played, and it’s one you can interact with at a level never seen before in the series. Yes, it was a long wait, but believe me when I say Rockstar has truly pushed the boat out (which, handily enough, is also something you can do yourself in GTA 6 if you find yourself beached).

I’ll readily admit I’m an easy mark for a game like this. I love action movies, car chases, and dad rock, and GTA 6 holds precisely the same things near and dear. I won’t list the long catalogue of movie references I’ve spotted since it’s way more satisfying to recognise them yourself. I also won’t spoil any of the specific needle drops Rockstar finds itself indulging in more than ever – one of which has become one of my favourite moments in the entire series. It does take over the dial a bit more than usual for key moments, but it’s always to great effect, and it certainly hasn’t come at the cost of any reduced focus on radio stations. The mammoth tracklist otherwise includes the return of classic stations V-Rock, Emotion, and Vice City FM, all of which are absolutely overflowing with solid gold (as is new metal station The Chamber). Just those four stations alone – which account for the lion’s share of my listening – feature nearly 200 songs between them.

In a considerable blow for any company trying to sell me a next-generation console in the near future, GTA 6 also looks even better than it sounds. Allow me to freely concede I’ve never been fussy about frame rates, so long as they don’t constantly fluctuate. For all the hand-wringing I’ve observed over the fact that GTA 6 is locked to 30 frames-per-second – just as Rockstar’s most recent cowboy masterpiece was, not for nothing – I simply did not care in the slightest while I was actually playing. What matters to me is that it looks absolutely incredible and runs smoothly and reliably on a standard PS5. I find all the brilliant visual flourishes far more important, from the concentric rings of ripples on water due to helicopter rotor downwash, to the almost imperceptible line of sweat that appears on Lucia’s forehead after a brisk jog, or the buckling of the fabric on a shirt as torsos twist, to the temporary dents on a punching bag as you strike it. It’s the way long hair rises, whips, and falls over a character’s shoulders and back, whether that’s Lucia’s ponytail swinging back and forth – or my Jason’s luxurious mullet hanging in the air over a motorcycle jump during its brief moment of zero gravity.

This level of detail is seen in other animations, too – dynamic fights which never appear to play out the same way, and the bespoke solutions for characters to slink along the side of a vehicle if the door can’t fully open. Like, there aren’t just animations for operating longarm weapons one-handed if your other hand is full; there’s a separate animation for opening drink cans with one hand as well.

If a sufficiently stable and properly paced 30fps is the route to GTA 6 looking and functioning the way it does, bug-free, then I have no complaints. The sheer density of traffic and pedestrians is stunning, and the graphics at night are supernaturally good. Rockstar allows the world to be realistically dark, giving the lighting room to really flex. It’s honestly jaw-dropping, whether that’s at street level with car headlights and taillights piercing the dark, down on the beach during a late evening storm, or from high above where every light source in the city seems to be individually visible from a distance. Just imagine Microsoft Flight Simulator, only after you land, you can leave the airport, hit a drive-thru, and grab a burger.

The feeling of authenticity is ever-present, and it extends across every element of what you see on screen. For instance, it’s not just that cars look incredible, or that they have animated drivetrains – which is something you don’t get in even the very best racing games. It’s that they’re not just cars – they’re all someone’s car. Maybe the bumper stickers have a story to tell, or there’s bespoke clutter in the tray or trunk. Maybe they belong to a specific business on the map; I’m still seeing vans driving around town with graphics and logos I haven’t noticed before. Maybe they’ve lived a hard life outside in the harsh Leonida sun, the clear coat has flaked away, and they now carry a patina of road grime and dust. Maybe the interior surfaces and seats are worn, maybe they’ve been poorly maintained and belch black exhaust smoke, or maybe they’ve been carefully customised with dazzling neons and truck nuts.

This attention to detail extends to boats, too. Not only have most of them been christened with unique names, but they too are filled with various personal belongings and custom fit-outs. And yes, they can be launched from trailers, put back on trailers, and towed to another boat ramp on the other side of the map if you wish. I adore this, and I suspect those who really want to roleplay in this world will too.

At any rate, GTA 6’s dedication to its in-universe car culture is honestly ludicrous, and I love it. There are tuning shops, car salerooms, and motorsport venues all over the map. The fully modelled engines can be restored and switched out. Exhaust and supercharger mods have noticeable effects on a car’s sound. Hell, there’s even a difference in the texture of a hasty Pay ’n’ Spray rush job, which always results in a visible orange peel effect, and a professional respray at a dedicated customisation shop.

The improvements to car damage are massive as well, with GTA 6 more closely resembling something like a slightly scaled-back Wreckfest rather than GTA 5 . Lights and mirrors fall off, panels bend and buckle dramatically, and entire wheels can be ripped off before your car becomes fully disabled. Belt an assailant’s head against a nearby car, and it’ll even crater realistically where they bounced off the metal.

Car handling is also the strongest it’s ever been in the series, and it feels a lot more like a refined version of GTA 4 than GTA 5, which is actually great news. It brings back a very tangible sense of heft, only without the overly exaggerated suspension wallow. You can really slide cars properly here, and throwing them into 90-degree corners and perching them on the throttle is now total Hollywood highlight reel stuff. The only thing that really gave me pause was the motorcycle handling, which is quite upright and stiff compared to previous GTAs – I don’t hate it, but it does feel like it comes from a different game altogether.

The decision to opt for more realistic street widths makes for a way more authentic and engaging driving experience, whether you’re cutting up cars on the freeway or cruising the busy beachside strip. GTA 6 is not afraid to trap you behind traffic or roadworks and force you into quick decisions. Do you take the footpath? Do you push through and risk damage? It’s always asking you to think and act, and creates a dynamic to keep you fully engaged.

After a certain point in the story, you’ll get full control to assign Jason and Lucia personal vehicles that actually speak to you, breaking from the preset personal vehicles Michael, Franklin, and Trevor had in GTA 5. For instance, my Jason’s main ride eventually became a fully-built, Marty McFly-style black truck that I sought out and customised specifically. I really appreciate being able to control this element, and you can eventually have a small fleet of personal vehicles at your disposal.

Your car in GTA 6 is very much like your horse in RDR 2, in that it will keep a variety of things safe for you when you’re not carrying (or wearing) them – like stash bags full of stolen goods, longarms, and a handful of outfits. No, you’re no longer able to pull a bazooka out of your back pocket – which may well be a point of contention amongst longtime players who crave the chaotic energy of having a stocked weapon wheel at their constant disposal – but I honestly haven’t missed it. I actually really like the RDR 2 approach of needing to gear up thoughtfully and manually, and it’s neat to see longarms slung over Jason and Lucia’s shoulders or held in their off hand.

Knowing how influential the more measured and deliberate pace of RDR 2 was set to be on GTA 6, I figured I had an idea of how this would translate into Rockstar’s modern crime universe – but even still I was unprepared for how satisfying the shift in attitude would be. It shepherded me into a more lifelike cadence, where I would wake up and eat breakfast or brew a coffee to buff my health, stamina, and focus (which is GTA 6’s consumable slow-motion power-up that functions similarly to Red Dead’s Dead Eye system). Following that, I may take on a story mission before spending the remainder of the day trying out a new fishing spot, playing pool at the bar, or simply exploring the area looking for cool vehicles, secrets, or interesting strangers.

It all very much feels like RDR 2 as well. Similar to Arthur, Jason and Lucia feel a little heavier than the GTA 5 trio in a pleasing way that grounds them more in the world and gives them a more convincing sensation of inertia as they otherwise seamlessly transition from one action to another. Opponents go down in ever-changing ways, depending on whether you’ve shot to kill or wound – and what you’ve shot them with. Heavy weapons will remove limbs entirely, so keep that in mind if you’re trying to be merciful. Hell, you can even pick up hats and sunglasses from your vanquished foes.

However, while RDR 2’s intimate, smoke-filled shootouts remain some of the best in the business, GTA 6’s firefights are typically orders of magnitude more spectacular thanks to the vastly increased amount of lead you can sling downrange. Gunning helicopters out of the sky is perhaps the most potent example, as sparks shower from the rotors, the mechanics fail, and they spiral down and either break into bits or disappear into enormous fireballs. Helicopters are actually more fragile than ever, and they’re especially susceptible to damage to their tail rotors, but I do love how much more realistic the crashes have subsequently become.

That said, there is a newfound focus on gently encouraging a slightly more empathetic approach when you deal with Leonida’s colourful locals – although, rest assured, the freedom to lash out like a heinous psychopath still exists. If you want to land a jumbo jet on the beach, you still can; you’ll just have to realistically find your way into the cockpit instead of teleporting in from the nose gear. From what I’ve gleaned, it might make sense to have a separate save file for these sorts of shenanigans if you want the story to culminate in a specific way (yes, there are multiple endings). In slightly disappointing news, it doesn’t appear there’s a way to replay previously completed missions from the mission list, which is an unexpected step back from the philosophy embraced by GTA 4: The Ballad of Gay Tony and GTA 5. There is an exhaustive list of cheats that are unveiled after completing the story, which is excellent to see since fun and hilarious cheats are a core part of GTA’s DNA. At least for now, however, the completed missions database is just a series of static thumbs.

The broad love for GTA 4’s Three Leaf Clover bank heist mission is typically regarded as an important trigger for GTA 5’s heavy focus on major heists, and that philosophy has been wonderfully continued in GTA 6. Several massive heists – each with prep work, moving parts, complementary roles for Jason and Lucia, and dramatic crescendos – are all excellent. They unfold within varied and impeccably detailed locations, they benefit greatly from the vastly improved shooting and driving, and they are rewardingly spaced out across the second half of the story. However, what’s particularly interesting is GTA 6’s own brand of Three Leaf Clover’s classic cops ’n’ robbers fantasy, where tense bank robberies aren’t just isolated to scripted missions you can only execute once per playthrough – they’re now something you can pull off in the open world, at will.

Now, you can’t just successfully roll over banks immediately; you need to graduate up to them later in the story once you have the equipment to deal with dye packs. Hit a target with marked bills (or yank an ATM from a wall with a winch) before you have the necessary gear and your take will be lost in an exploding bloom of pink soot that totally coats Jason and/or Lucia and will persistently smear the inside of any vehicle cabin. It’s actually a brilliant visual effect for something I anticipate we’ll all overtly avoid doing more than once.

However, once banks do become viable targets, all bets are off. Essentially speaking, it’s Three Leaf Clover whenever you want . No more walking past locked bank branches that can only be engaged with in one-off story missions; now banks are realistic locations that can be entered and cleaned out. That’s a genuinely powerful shift in the long-established GTA crime fantasy. There’s more to it than checking a box and adding another law you can break; it’s about making this living, breathing world around you make more sense than ever. As much as I adore GTA 5, it is invariably discordant that you can bust into a military base and steal a tank, but you can’t push open a door and rob a bank. In GTA 6, that hard-to-swallow imbalance is gone. You can simply do both.

Bank jobs in the open world can unfold in multiple ways. Maybe you successfully sneak in the back, find the safe code, get distracted by an office cat, and get sprung by the staff. Maybe you tail an armoured truck pulling up, meaning the vault will be open – making for a bigger payday, plus access to safe deposit boxes. Maybe you stumble in with zero plan, stick around way too long, and completely botch your getaway. Robbing a bank solo typically works out differently from robbing it with your CPU-controlled partner by your side; for instance, head in alone and security might be a little less inclined to outright surrender.

Luke Reilly's 25 Favourite Open-World Action/Driving Games

What I find particularly satisfying, however, is how smart you can indeed play it with a little planning. For instance, I’ve been finding banks within a few blocks of multi-storey parking lots great targets to focus on. I park Jason or Lucia’s personal car a few levels up, steal a random getaway ride, and head to the bank. After taking it down, I head straight back to the parking lot as the cops mount their response. After speeding a few floors up, stashing the cash, and changing outfits (you can store a selection of spare clothes in your cars), I can gently cruise past the cops blocking the exit and make a completely clean exfil.

I’m absolutely loving the new, nuanced Wanted system, where the cops can only act on the information they have. I think it’s actually going to be a little frustrating to go back to the likes of GTA 5, where the police magically make a beeline towards you when your crimes cross a certain threshold – even if there are no witnesses, or any believable way for them to know which car you’re driving or what you look like.

There is no longer a radar showing the location of approaching cops, and I haven’t missed it once. Not knowing where the police could be turns evasion into a whole new and more organic experience, where the focus is on scanning the actual world in front of you for threats rather than spending most of your time looking at the minimap. That is, you’re no longer just trying to choose the right streets to leave a hot zone, like Pac-Man trying to route away from the nearest ghosts. You’re listening to the scanner for hints about what the cops know. You’re eyeballing the traffic in the distance, trying to figure out if any of them are police cruisers. It’s knowing when and where to stay out of view entirely, and when it’s safe for you to hide in plain sight. That’s a far bigger thrill.

articles.title: GTA 6: How Microtransactions and GTA + Benefits Work
articles.summary: How do the GTA+ benefits work in GTA 6? We've got the answers.
articles.body:
Anyone who pre-ordered GTA 6 is entitled to one free month of GTA +, Rockstar’s subscription service. It's been around for a while now, proving worthwhile for fans of GTA Online who get exclusive items and opportunities in the game through it, as well as access to a library of the developer’s games, including the likes of GTA 5, Red Dead Redemption, and Bully. But it also comes with fresh benefits for those playing GTA 6.

These bonuses include store discounts, exclusive vehicles, and ways to make earning in-game cash easier. It’s not quite pay-to-win due to the small advantages it gives and GTA 6’s nature as a single-player game, but it will certainly give a leg up to those with a GTA+ subscription.

All of the listed benefits, which can be found on the in-game store page, can be found here:

Venturas BLVD Elegy & Garage – A free ‘90 Annis Venturas BLVD Elegy, specially tuned and featuring an exclusive widebody design, as well as access to a single-car garage to store it, located in the Crosstown area of Vice City. This garage also includes a weapon locker and the ability to directly fence stolen items. These are only available from Chapter 3 of the story onward.

Transit Services Bonuses – Scooter Bros Premium vehicle care, RydeMe rideshare app premium membership, free scooter, bike, and Seashark rentals, plus free rides on all Leonida public transport.

Increased Sell Value – Benefit from a 10% increase on all eligible owned vehicle sales.

Store Discounts – Get a 10% discount at select businesses, including weapons and clothes shops, hairdressers, tattooists, vehicle mod shops, and more.

Crucially, if you have signed up for GTA+, but want to experience the purest form of GTA 6 possible, these benefits can be switched off in the game’s settings menu. The pre-order bonus must be redeemed before March 31, 2027, and will renew automatically unless cancelled, costing $7.99/£6.99 per month after that. Of course, we are yet to hear anything about GTA 6’s potential online component, and how GTA+ may play into that equation.

GTA 6 Vintage Vice City Pack Screenshots

All GTA 6 pre-orders also come with the Vintage Vice City, which can be purchased separately if you’re planning to buy the game after launch. Here are the details on what’s included, all of which become available in Chapter 3 of the story .

‘55 Vapid Stanier & Garage – A classic yellow and white sedan that can be stored in the Shore Court garage near Ocean Beach. You can collect it from the iconic Ocean View Hotel, which features prominently in GTA: Vice City.

Outfits & Hairstyles — Jason’s vintage pastel coloured linen suit and Lucia’s red sequin mini dress can be paired with two 80s-inspired hairstyles for the couple. These become available once you’ve picked up the Stanier and can be found in any wardrobe or at any hairdresser.

Exclusive Weapon Pattern — Most guns can be wrapped in a tropical pattern inspired by Vice City protagonist Tommy Vercetti’s iconic palm tree shirt. Available from any Ammu-Nation store once you’ve picked up the Stanier.

If you bought the Ultimate Edition , then we have a list of all of the bonuses that come with that listed here, as well as when in the game you can gain access to those exclusive vehicles, weapons, and cosmetics.

We’ve got plenty more GTA 6 for you here at IGN. You can check out our review , or head over to our launch live blog , where I’ll be doing my best to answer as many of your spoiler-free questions as you may have about the game.

Simon Cardy is a Senior Editor at IGN who can mainly be found skulking around open world games, indulging in Korean cinema, or despairing at the state of Tottenham Hotspur and the New York Jets. Follow him on Bluesky at @cardy.bsky.social .

articles.title: How GTA 6 Came Together at Rockstar North
articles.summary: Current Rockstar North Co-Studio Head and Head of Development Rob Nelson seems relaxed for a man in Rockstar North’s bridge, essentially moments from steering what may well be the most anticipated entertainment product launch of all time into port — after 13 long years, no less.
articles.body:
Current Rockstar North Co-Studio Head and Head of Development Rob Nelson seems relaxed for a man in Rockstar North’s bridge, essentially moments from steering what may well be the most anticipated entertainment product launch of all time into port — after 13 long years, no less.

What’s perhaps more interesting, however, is how even Nelson is quite happy to concede that not even he quite knows how a game as fundamentally huge and absolutely astonishing as GTA 6 has come together so magically. Money and talent is only a part of the answer; the rest is perhaps a little more nebulous.

“I think it takes a lot of obstinance, really,” explains Nelson. “Just a sort of stubborn persistence in pursuit of the same thing for a long time, and a team that’s been together for a really long time. Now a really, really long time.

“And the answer is I don’t know. I mean, I only know my part of it, which is a part of it. And the stuff that [co-studio head] Aaron [Garbutt] does, and the stuff that [director of technology] Phil [Hooker] does, and the stuff that the programming team does, I don’t know. They just do it and we sort of build it up in layers.”

Nelson explains that Hooker sent an update through to the team very recently that showcased the progress of missions, areas, and features in the game over the last few years, and says it was “shocking to see how far it’s come.”

“Well, unfortunately, lots of people saw it in the hack that we had a few years ago — where [the game] was,” he says. “And I think in development you forget that. You forget the doldrums that you go through and you just sort of cling on to little wins every day, day by day or week by week. Sometimes they feel few and far between — certainly when you’re a few years out. And it’s just trust in the people that you’ve worked with for a long time that they’re going to hold up their end of it.”

“And this game had to rely on that. It probably sounds like a cliché answer, but this team and this game needed that more than we’ve ever had, because we’re larger than we’ve ever been — double the size that we were on RDR 2 — more spread out than we’ve ever been in terms of studios all over the world. Time zones. COVID.

“And you sit in it for week after week and just go, ‘Is this thing ever going to come together? Are we ever going to find it?’ But I think because we’ve been pursuing the same thing for a long time, every team knows what they generally want to do and want to evolve, and they just get on with it. And we work in these sort of eight-week sprints and pull a bunch of stuff together, evaluate it, make a bunch of notes, go back, iterate, iterate, iterate.”

Teams getting on with it appears to be precisely how fantastic and unexpected flourishes make their way to the final product. I note an example, which is the fact that there's now a unique animation solution for characters to get out of cars in skinny gaps, when the door can’t open all the way. Nelson lights up.

“There’s so many examples of it across the game, but that is a great example of one where the team just does their thing,” he says. “That hit a build one day and I played it just like you played it. And I was, like, ‘Holy shit, look at this. It’s amazing.’ I never asked for it. As far as I know, none of the other heads of development asked for it. The team did it. The animation directors decided that they wanted to do it.

“And that’s the most exciting thing, I think, for this team working on this stuff. It’s that there’s so many talented and experienced people working on it, and caring equally about their part, that every build is exciting. That’s I think what sustains you. It’s like every time you get a new build and there’s new stuff hitting it. It gives you energy to keep going.

“And it can be anything. It could be new ads on the radio, or just the radio going live for the first time. It can be new UI elements coming in to try, or little touches like that and you go, ‘Okay, all right, we’re just going to keep going.’ But, yeah, that’s a great example of something that just the team did off their own back.”

Nelson concedes that this approach does have to be managed, because without any guardrails, “every team will go crazy and go on forever.”

“And so there’s a bit of a contract there between all of us, including ourselves; having checks and balances in terms of where we push, how far we push, how hard we push, and how much resource [something] is worth, because everything is time and resource spent,” he says. “And contrary to what people think, we don’t have infinite money or time, or resource. So we do have to make decisions.”

On the topic of decisions, Rockstar’s confirmation that GTA 6 runs at 30 frames per second across all platforms including PS5 Pro became a popular talking point last week. Speaking with Nelson about what would have to fundamentally change about GTA 6 – and when – if the game had targeted 60fps, the Rockstar North veteran has a very simple answer.

“Too much, too much,” he says “It wouldn’t have been acceptable to anybody. The simple answer is, when you ask the technical team, they’re, like, ‘Have you seen it?’ There’s too many compromises that would’ve had to have been made to do that, is the short answer.”

In simple terms, the frame rate had to be limited somewhere in order to achieve Rockstar’s artistic vision. While the team is not ruling out things being different on future hardware, GTA 6’s sheer amount of visual fidelity, the complexity of its simulation, and the amount of systems and gameplay options it has would simply not be possible on current hardware at higher frame rate.

After playing it for the last three weeks I can’t imagine removing anything. Interestingly, it appears Nelson plays GTA 6 in an extremely similar way to the style of play I settled into during the review period – particularly in the way he prepares prior to open-world store and bank heists.

“I love just going into a store and buying a six-pack and walking down the street, drinking them one at a time, getting progressively more belligerent ’til I’m throwing the last two and talking to people,” grins Nelson. “And then I’ll call Lucia and see if she wants to hang out and sort of walk around”

“Just watching the world, the city, pass from day to night and seeing the population change and seeing people out for a night out. I think it’s that. I think it’s the fact that you can really feel like you’re embodying your version of these characters in that world. And then you could go from playing that solo to being on a date and walking around holding hands, and you can stroll down the beach or go into a nightclub and dance together, or go robbing together.”

As I discovered myself over the last few weeks, Nelson explains that the amount of preparation you want to do typically determines how successful your crime spree will be.

“I like to get just all of it ready,” he says. “I’ll just get a big vehicle, a big truck that I’ve souped up that can hold six bags, and I’ll park it somewhere close by. Then I’ll go steal a motorcycle that I don’t own and park it really close to where I’m going to go rob, go in and rob it, come out, take off on the motorcycle, stash the bags in the truck, go hit some more, [and] load the truck up with bags. Then you could either send your partner to go fence it, or go fence them yourself.”

IGN’s GTA 6 review is live now . We also have a GTA 6 launch live blog so you don’t miss a thing.

Luke Reilly is an award-winning journalist with 23 years of media experience. He previously served as Editor of Official PlayStation Magazine – Australia and Australian 360, before joining IGN in 2011. You can find him on Bluesky @mrlukereilly to ask him things about stuff.

articles.title: GTA 6 Is Now the Joint-Highest Rated Game of All Time
articles.summary: GTA 6 has become the joint-highest rated game of all time, following the widespread publication of reviews.
articles.body:
GTA 6 has become the joint-highest rated game of all time, following the widespread publication of reviews in the past hour.

Rockstar's masterpiece currently sits with an all-time best score of 99 on Metacritic , an honor shared only with Nintendo's original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time release back in 1997 on N64, almost 30 years ago. No other game since has managed such a feat. (The new version of Ocarina for Switch 2 managed a paltry score of just 96.)

While both the N64 version of Ocarina and GTA 6 share a 99 average, GTA 6 has impressively managed to pull this off with more than six times' the number of reviews — over 120 at the time of writing, with over 100 of those listed with a perfect score. And while it's possible GTA 6's ranking could still slip down a point as more reviews are published, it would still be the best-rated game in nearly three decades.

Few others titles released in the recent memory have come anywhere close to this — though if you head back to the last console generation, Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Super Mario Odyssey both managed a 97 average, a standing they share with Rockstar's own Red Dead Redemption 2.

IGN's GTA 6 review is of course now live, and also returned a perfect 10/10 score. We described it as "exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered," as well as "unprecedented, unbelievable and unmissable."

IGN has everything you need for the launch of GTA 6, including the GTA 6 global release times , as well as details on the last-minute PS5 update you'll need to download . In case you missed it, last night we learned the real-life identity of GTA 6's Lucia . And we're now live with our GTA 6 launch blog , which we'll use to fill you in on everything else about the game over the coming hours.

articles.title: GTA 6 Xbox Series S Performance: How Does the Weakest Console Handle the Biggest Game of All Time?
articles.summary: GTA 6 is finally here, and one of the biggest questions heading up to launch is how well the Xbox Series S would handle the game – well, I've finally had the chance to play the game on the tiny Xbox.
articles.body:
GTA 6 is finally here , and one of the biggest questions heading up to launch is how well the Xbox Series S would handle the game. I've finally had the chance to play the game on the tiny Xbox.

Rockstar announced a couple weeks ago that all versions of GTA 6 would be "targeting" 30fps . While it's disappointing that even the PS5 Pro won't be able to hit 60 fps, that performance is about what I expected from the Xbox Series S. And while I wait for my frame rate analysis to stop running on my first clip of the game, the Xbox Series S version actually seems pretty decent, all things considered.

The Xbox Series S obviously doesn't have the same graphics treats that the PS5 Pro version of the game has, but even without the ray traced shadows and the PSSR, the game holds up well on the 1440p machine. Character models are still extremely detailed, and even has some decent subsurface scattering and the environments are incredibly beautiful, no doubt learning from Rockstar's time with Red Dead Redemption 2.

But where the Xbox Series S falls short is in the finer details. The edge of nearly every surface is aliased, almost looking like there's a border of static around every character and building, particularly around people's hair. There's also an early scene on a boat, where Jason's face is noticeably soft until it zooms closer in, no doubt to save on some GPU resources. But, GTA 6 on the Xbox Series S is using FSR 4 to upscale from 720p up to 1080p, so some softness is to be expected.

Through the intro of the game, GTA 6 typically sits right at 30fps on the Xbox Series S, and it's surprisingly smooth. However, there are certain parts of the game – like when Lucia pulls out a gun in one of the first scenes – where the frame rate drops. Usually, these drops are very minor, but I did notice a couple of drops as low as 24fps, according to Trdrop. However, I will say that I didn't really notice most of them.

I didn't get early access to GTA 6, so all of this is based on the first section of the game. The real test of GTA 6's performance is going to be how it handles some of the wild scenes that are sure to come in the later parts of the game. But, any action game needs to nail the calmer moments if it wants any chance of standing up when you're surrounded by explosions and gunfire, and when it comes to GTA 6 on the Xbox Series S, it mostly nails that baseline. The game looks great, considering the level of hardware available, but you will definitely notice the difference if you put it side-by-side with something like the PS5 Pro.

As GTA 6's launch unfolds, we'll be live blogging the game , watching for all the weird and wild stuff that the community finds. IGN also gave GTA 6 a perfect 10, where reviewer Luke Reilly calls it "exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played. " For everything else GTA 6, stay tuned to IGN.

Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her @Jackiecobra

articles.title: GTA 6 reviews say highly-anticipated game is a masterpiece
articles.summary: Critics have their say as to whether GTA 6, the most anticipated video game of all time, lives up to the hype.
articles.body:
After 13 years of waiting, record-breaking trailers and lengthy delays, critics have given their answer to one of the year's biggest questions.

Does Grand Theft Auto 6, surely the most anticipated game of all time, live up to the hype?

According to the first reviews, it's a resounding yes.

Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 - tying with Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record since 1998.

Reviewers overwhelmingly agreed the open-world action game was an ambitious, ground-breaking title that was well worth the wait.

Not everyone is enjoying the glowing praise - with some posters to online forums objecting to what one called "the ultra fan-boy hype."

But there is no question the reviewers have been effusive with their praise, with gaming website IGN branding GTA 6 "unprecedented", "unbelievable" and "unmissable".

Meanwhile in its five star review, Eurogamer said makers Rockstar had "pushed back the horizon of video games once again" with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

"The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome," reviewer Chris Tapsell wrote , but he added "there are also nits to pick".

For The New York Times one of those nits was whether the realism of the game might dull the fun chaos of its predecessors.

Reviewer Yussef Cole said GTA 6 had "matured beyond its memorable car crashes and stickups" with consequences to every action.

But "some of my favourite moments have been careening through streets with squad cars in hot pursuit," he wrote.

The graphics of the game were hotly anticipated and so far have not disappointed critics, with The Guardian describing Leonida, the setting inspired by Miami, as "so lifelike that at times it beggars belief".

And the relationship between the lead characters, Jason and Lucia, has also stunned critics.

"They feel like real people rather than puppets dancing to your whim," The Guardian's Keza MacDonald wrote, adding: "I found it impossible not to care for them".

Writing for Forbes , Paul Tassi said: "I can't say I've ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share".

The Washington Post said GTA 6 "raises the bar at every level", while Bloomberg 's Jason Schreier called it a "masterpiece" in his five star review.

"It's hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here," he wrote. "There's nothing else like it.

"While playing this game, I often found myself wondering how it even exists."

Rockstar hasn't revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

The Game Awards - the most watched ceremony of its kind in the industry - gave players a teaser of the critical reception when its 2026 nominations were revealed on Tuesday.

And despite having not released at the time, GTA 6 was the most-nominated title.

It will be up for eight prizes, including game of the year and best music.

The nomination of Manni L Perez in the best performance category confirmed wide speculation that she is the actress behind main character Lucia in GTA 6 - a fact Rockstar hadn't previously officially confirmed.

The jury for the event is largely made up of gaming journalists around the world, who would have received advanced copies for review.

Some, though, have questioned how a game that has just been released has garnered such positive reviews and award nominations.

There is a view in some online forums that the hype around the game has got out of control as, with one poster commenting: "I think everyone's tired of hearing about this game - I don't even want to play it anymore."

It appears so far, however, that is likely to be very much a minority view.

articles.title: GTA 6 Will Never Get a 60fps Update on PlayStation Pro as It's 'Not Powerful Enough'
articles.summary: There's bad news for any GTA 6 fans still hoping for a 60fps option on PlayStation 5 Pro.
articles.body:
There's bad news for any GTA 6 fans still hoping for a 60fps option on PlayStation 5 Pro.

While Sony's beefier PS5 is arguably the most powerful console on the market today, even it is unable to run Rockstar's new masterpiece at 60fps. That's according to the game's technology production director Marc Chambers, who admitted that the PS5 Pro could only do so much.

Somewhat controversially, GTA 6 targets 30fps across all of its supported console platforms, with the same rate on everything from the under-powered Xbox Series S all the way up to PS5 Pro.

Naturally, there are other differences — and the game's PS5 Pro version has a few extra bells and whistles. But anyone expecting a better frame rate will need to temper their expectations — at least, perhaps, until the game's PC version arrives.

"While the PS5 Pro's central processor is slightly better than the PS5 base console, it is not powerful enough to run the game's complex simulation at higher frame rates," Chambers told Kotaku .

That said, PS5 Pro still offers other improvements, he continued. "Our base presentation makes use of ray-traced reflections and global illumination," Chambers noted. "On the PS5 Pro, this is enhanced with the addition of ray-traced shadows, as well as overall added clarity through the use of PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR). The PS5 Pro features an upgraded graphics processor and upscaling technology that we leverage to increase the game's visual fidelity."

Speaking to IGN, Rockstar's co-studio head and head of development Rob Nelson said that "too much" of GTA 6 would have to fundamentally change for the game to target 60fps. "Too much, too much," he said in our big GTA 6 interview that went live today . "It wouldn’t have been acceptable to anybody. The simple answer is, when you ask the technical team, they're, like, 'Have you seen it?' There’s too many compromises that would've had to have been made to do that, is the short answer."

Today also brings more detail on how GTA 6 fares while running on Xbox Series S , where it is one of the first games to use AMD's FSR 4.1 on Xbox to upscale the graphically demanding game from 720p to 1080p.

IGN has everything you need for the launch of GTA 6, including the GTA 6 global release times , as well as details on the last-minute PS5 update you'll need to download . In case you missed it, last night we learned the real-life identity of GTA 6's Lucia . And we're now live with our GTA 6 launch blog , which we'll use to fill you in on everything else about the game over the coming hours.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
articles.summary: Will Wright is working on a new game called MyMems that’s built around AI and exploring your own memories.
articles.body: Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge. The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others. Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.” [Image: I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.” Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles. Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards. Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.” [Image: “We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says. MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game. “It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you? Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.” Update, November 18th: Added context about Artificial Agency.

articles.title: Spirit of the Shadows: Experience the Entire First Issue of the Hit Horror Series
articles.summary: Oni Press' Spirit of the Shadows is easily one of the most visually stunning new comics of 2026, and now you can read the entire first issue for free.
articles.body:
Late last year, IGN debuted a preview of Spirit of the Shadows , a visually stunning horror series from Oni Press. That very psychedelic comic turned out to be one of the real joys of 2026, and now it's available in bookstores as a trade paperback collected edition.

With that in mind, IGN is now able to feature the entire first issue of Spirit of the Shadows. Check it out in the slideshow gallery below and decide for yourself if this is a comic for you:

Spirit of the Shadows #1 - Full Issue Gallery

Spirit of the Shadows is a collaboration between Nick Cagnetti and Daniel Ziegler. Here's the official summary of the book:

EMBRACE YOUR FEAR . . . THE SPIRIT OF THE SHADOWS DRAWS NEAR! From the darkest recesses within acclaimed cartoonist Nick Cagnetti (Archie, Pink Lemonade) and co-creator Daniel Ziegler (Elodie) comes the most visually stunning, outrageously otherworldly, and hauntingly heartfelt superhero-horror hit of the decade!

Once, Erik Leroux was a mortal musician, selflessly devoted to his music and his true love, Katrina . . . until his sudden death plunged his soul into the carnival- like torments of the spirit world beyond our own. Now, reborn as a phantom with fleeting memories of his life among the living, and forever cursed to bear the arcane costume his corpse wore to the grave, Erik will claw his way back from the infernal planes to uncover the mysteries of his own life . . . and avenge the dark sins that transformed him into the SPIRIT OF THE SHADOWS!

“I guarantee you're not going to find another comic on the stands right now quite like this one—from the story to the art, my friend Daniel and I really tried to create something cohesive and evocative in the way that only this medium can provide,” said Cagnetti in his original statement. “To achieve that, I put a lot of care into differentiating styles and techniques for each of the settings the story goes to make them each feel distinct. You're swept up in this dreamlike haze alongside the main character, and you go through all the emotions and revelations alongside him. The end result should really make for a rewarding experience you can reread and look at completely differently the next time, but I'm envious for readers to experience that ride for the first time here soon!”

The trade paperback for Spirit of the Shadows is available in bookstores now. You can order a copy on Amazon .

For more, check out an exclusive preview of The Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost Mine and a preview of the Image Comics graphic novel Content .
